column2: On the authority of al-Nawwās ibn Samʿān (may Allah be pleased with him), from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: “Righteousness is good character, and sin is what wavers in your soul and you dislike people coming to know of it.” Reported by Muslim.

And on the authority of Wābiṣah ibn Maʿbad (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: I came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and he said: “You have come to ask about righteousness and sin?” I said: “Yes.”

He said: “Consult your heart. Righteousness is that with which the soul is at peace and the heart is at peace, and sin is what wavers in the soul and goes back and forth in the breast, even if people give you a ruling and give you rulings again.” A ḥasan hadith; we have narrated it in the Musnads of the two imams Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal and al-Dārimī with a ḥasan chain.

The hadith of al-Nawwās was reported by Muslim. The hadith of Wābiṣah was reported by Aḥmad and al-Dārimī, and its chain has been criticised, but it has supporting narrations with good chains, which the ḥāfiẓ Ibn Rajab mentions in Jāmiʿ al-ʿUlūm wa-l-Ḥikam; on the whole it is similar to the hadith of al-Nawwās ibn Samʿān.

Righteousness (birr) is a comprehensive word covering the inward matters in the heart and the outward matters on the tongue and the limbs. The verse “Righteousness is not that you turn your faces…” [al-Baqarah 2:177] clearly indicates this,

for its beginning contains the inward matters and its end the outward matters. Birr is also used specifically for dutifulness to parents, especially when paired with ṣilah, in which case the two mean dutifulness to parents and maintaining ties of kinship. Birr also comes paired with taqwā,

as in the saying of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic: “And cooperate in righteousness and piety” [al-Māʾidah 5:2]. When they come together, as in this verse, birr is explained as doing acts of obedience
and taqwā as leaving what is forbidden; and when either is mentioned on its own, it covers both meanings together. This is like islām and īmān, and faqīr and miskīn.

The hadith of al-Nawwās says, “Righteousness is good character.” Good character may mean specifically the noble trait known by this name, righteousness being explained by it because of its importance and great standing, like “The religion is sincere counsel” and “Ḥajj is ʿArafah”;

or it may be meant in a general and comprehensive sense for everything good. This is indicated by the way the Mother of the Believers, ʿĀʾishah (may Allah be pleased with her), described the character of the Messenger ﷺ as being the Qurʾān, meaning that he adopted its manners, carried out its commands and avoided its prohibitions.

His words, “and sin is what wavers in your soul and you dislike people coming to know of it”: some sin is plain and clear, and some wavers in the breast, the soul is not at peace with it, and a person dislikes people coming to know of it,

because it is something one is ashamed to do, so the one who does it fears people's tongues attacking him. This resembles what was said in three earlier hadiths: “Whoever guards against the doubtful matters has kept his religion and his honour free of blame”;
“Leave what gives you doubt for what does not give you doubt”; and “Among the words that people have received from the earliest prophethood is: If you feel no shame, then do as you wish.”

Sin (ithm) means sins in general, both clear and doubtful. It comes paired with ʿudwān (aggression), as in the saying of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic: “But do not cooperate in sin and aggression” [al-Māʾidah 5:2]; ʿudwān is then explained as transgression and injustice, which includes transgressing against people in their lives, wealth and honour.

In the hadith of Wābiṣah, righteousness is explained as that with which the soul is at peace and the heart is at peace. No difference between the two is apparent to me; the second clause may be emphasising the first,
since they agree in meaning. Sin is explained in it as the opposite of that, which is the same meaning by which sin is explained in the hadith of al-Nawwās.

His words at the beginning of the hadith of Wābiṣah, “Consult your heart”, and at its end, “even if people give you a ruling and give you rulings again”, show that what contains doubt and uncertainty, and with which the heart is not at peace,

is safer left, even if people have given rulings permitting it. What is meant is that a person of faith who fears Allah and is mindful of Him does not venture upon something his heart is not at peace with.
The ruling may come from someone without knowledge, or from someone with knowledge, but there is no clear evidence in the matter on which one can rely in acting.
But if there is evidence in the matter from the Book and the Sunnah, one is bound to follow it. And consulting the heart does not apply to the people of wickedness and sin,
for some of them commit sins openly and are not ashamed before Allah or His creation; such people fall into what is clearly unlawful, let alone what is doubtful.

In the hadith of Wābiṣah, the Prophet ﷺ tells him what he has come to ask about before he voices his question. This is to be understood—and Allah knows best—as the Prophet ﷺ already knowing of this Companion's concern to learn about righteousness and sin;
perhaps he had previously consulted the Prophet ﷺ about some part of this.
Good character is of great importance.
Righteousness and sin are comprehensive words.
In the matters of his religion, a Muslim goes ahead with what is clearly lawful and not with what is doubtful.
A believer who fears Allah does not do what his heart is not at peace with, even if he is given a ruling permitting it, unless it is something clear in the Sharīʿah, such as concessions.
The Companions (may Allah be pleased with them) were eager to know the lawful and the unlawful, righteousness and sin.
